title: The Near-Coup at Nvidia and the War on Open-Source AI
content:
On November 18 the AI company Anthropic priced its first public sale of stock at $81.3 billion, the largest IPO on record, against about $900 billion it has promised to spend. Six days earlier Jensen Huang was out as chief executive of Nvidia, the company he co-founded, in what I call a coup. In between, Washington filed a new rule on AI chips in the name of stopping China. Then, on November 19, Trump met Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
On November 23 Nvidia announced that its board had put Huang back in the job, 11 days after he resigned, and the President called it “the correct and proper decision.”
The motive starts with that bill: Anthropic is going to have to raise its prices to pay it. Open models stand in the way. A model is the AI program itself, and an open one is free: anyone can download it and run it on a computer they own. Jensen Huang was the most powerful American backer of open models.
The closed labs, companies like Anthropic that only rent their models out, need the rent and Washington wants the off switch, and a model you own gives them neither. You’ve been told this is America against China. There is no China versus the US. It is about technocrats weaponizing patriotism to support closed-source AI surveillance systems. On September 30, 2025, I said on air that the technocracy is global. Technocracy is the idea that we’re too stupid to make our own decisions, so scientists and engineers, and now AI, should make them for us. The fight is technocracy versus free will.
I Build with Both Kinds of AI
One person with AI sounds like a dude using ChatGPT. I was that dude myself once. I’ve been using AI since 2023, and I’ve been working on it a lot longer than that, since the early 1990s, when I was in high school and part of Duke University’s Talent Identification Program. All told I’ve put more than 5,000 hours into AI, with many sessions running side by side, and used about fifty different models.
In about a year and a half I’ve directed AI to write about 1.5 million lines of code across 11 projects, plus about a third as much again in automated tests, code whose only job is to check the rest. Nine of those projects are public websites, including my show’s site, Technocracy Atlas and DitchTheDollar. I make music videos with AI too, among them a song about surveillance and the land.
I don’t rent my data. I downloaded the original files myself, and they live on my own machines as one library I can search: 7,854 books, thousands of audio recordings and videos turned into text, court and government documents, a leaked set of offshore-company records and my show’s archive. For Technocracy Atlas I downloaded the federal government’s raw file on foreign-owned farmland, 49,548 rows, and had a program work out New Hampshire’s number from it. It matched the checked figures on all 11 points, with no AI doing the math.
My Mac Studio runs 171 jobs by itself, some on a schedule and some around the clock. One cuts every episode of my show into clips and posts them: 1,475 clips from 94 episodes so far, hundreds of them posted by the system itself. I also built 207 panels of AI advisers that imitate experts in different fields; they review the work and give me options, and I make the call.
What One Person Has Built with AI
Most people know AI as a chat window: you type a question and it answers. An AI employee is more like someone on your staff. You hand it a job and it does the work on its own. It thinks with an AI model, the program that serves as its brain. I’m building a whole team of them. The first version had 55, built on free open-source software called Hermes Agent, which anyone can download and change.
It didn’t always work at first, and in October I set it aside. When a project gets stuck, I leave the stuck part alone and keep tinkering. I try each new model on that part as it comes out, and I don’t bang my head against the wall in the meantime. A little more work and a newer model can take an old project and bring it back to life.
And it matters who owns that brain, because the owner decides what the employee is allowed to do and whether it shows up for work at all. So I’m rebuilding the team on the newest version of Hermes, and every employee will think with an open model on my own machines, with no closed lab behind it.
I pay the closed labs, and I’ve been censored by them. I hold the top plans at both Anthropic and OpenAI. Anthropic’s coding tool once refused to build me a program to collect drug package inserts, and those are public information. The image models refused about 80% of a batch of memes I tried to make for my show in November 2025.
What Closed Means
A closed model runs on someone else’s servers, and it can be switched off with a letter. On June 12, 2026, a letter signed by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ordered Anthropic to restrict access to Mythos and Fable, two of the AI models it sells, for foreign nationals. Anthropic had no way to check each user’s citizenship on the spot, so it switched both models off for everyone. Fable, the model I was using, stayed off for 18 days.
Back in October 2025 I’d warned on my show that if you use AI online, “it can always be cut off.” Within eight months it happened to me. The letter used the power in a 2018 export law to control emerging technologies, which had never been the basis for a control before and has no rules written for it, so it comes down to one man’s say-so.
The models came back after Anthropic agreed, Lutnick’s letter said, to inform the US government of any malicious activity, and he kept the right to bring the restriction back “should circumstances change or should Anthropic fail to adhere to its commitments.” To me, the model that came back was less intelligent and more restrictive. Anthropic said it was giving certain government partners more early access to both models. Lutnick said in September, “we trust Anthropic.”
Anthropic’s chief told the Senate in 2023, “when you control a model and you’re deploying it, you have the ability to monitor its usage.” Put the switch-off and the agreement to report next to that sentence. I call it a closed-source AI surveillance system.
What Washington Promised
The United States, far from promoting free markets and competition, is using government policy to protect Big Tech. The White House published “America’s AI Action Plan” in July 2025, and under the heading “Encourage Open-Source and Open-Weight AI” it says open models “have unique value for innovation because startups can use them flexibly without being dependent on a closed model provider.” Open-weight means the lab hands out the trained model itself, called its weights, so anyone can download it and run it on a computer he owns. The plan also says “the Federal government should create a supportive environment for open models.”
Then look at what they did. Trump’s order of December 11, 2025, tells the Commerce Secretary to list “onerous” state AI laws, cuts the listed states off from some federal broadband money and has the Attorney General set up a task force whose “sole responsibility” is to challenge state AI laws that conflict with the order’s policy. The chip rule of November 16 points the same way: the license it demands for advanced chips “will not apply” to chips going to companies headquartered in the United States. To me, both clear the road for the biggest American companies.
Senator Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) released a 291-page draft bill in March 2026, named the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act. Under it, nobody could release or deploy an advanced AI model, open source included, unless the developer was in the Energy Department’s program and handed the Secretary “the underlying code,” the “data used to train” it and its “model weights” on request. Break that rule and the fine would be “not less than $1,000,000 per day of the violation.” Rules like this would fall hardest on the free models, because a closed lab that charges for every use can pay for the lawyers and carry that risk,

report.summary: An opinion piece argues that a brief ouster of Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Anthropic's record IPO and new federal rules reveal a coordinated push against open-source AI models.
report.background: The article's backdrop is the money and policy stakes around frontier AI. Anthropic, a closed lab that rents access to its models, reportedly priced its IPO at $81.3 billion against roughly $900 billion in promised spending — economics that only work if usage stays metered and paid for. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run on their own hardware, undercut that model because they cannot be metered, monitored or switched off. In parallel, Washington has tightened export controls on advanced AI chips in the name of national security, while the White House's July 2025 'America's AI Action Plan' publicly endorsed open-source and open-weight AI, saying startups should not be dependent on a closed provider. The author contends these strands are connected: closed labs carrying enormous capital costs benefit from rules that raise compliance burdens on free alternatives, while chip and preemption policy concentrate capability among large US-headquartered firms. Note that the piece is an opinion essay; several of its specific claims are the author's own reporting and interpretation rather than independently verified fact.
key_points: The 'coup' narrative: The author says Jensen Huang left Nvidia on November 12 and was reinstated by the board on November 23, with the President calling the reversal 'the correct and proper decision.' He frames Huang as the most powerful American backer of open models and reads the episode as a fight over that stance — an interpretation the article asserts rather than documents.

The money motive: Anthropic's record IPO and roughly $900 billion spending pledge mean it must raise prices, and free downloadable models are the main competitive check on that pricing. On this reading, closed labs have a direct commercial interest in regulation that makes open weights harder to release, host or distribute.

Policy contradiction: The July 2025 AI Action Plan praises open models, yet the November 16 chip rule exempts US-headquartered firms from licensing, a December 11 order targets 'onerous' state AI laws and cuts some federal broadband money, and a 291-page draft Blackburn bill would require developers to hand over source code, training data and weights on request, with fines of at least $1 million per day.

The switch-off precedent: A June 12, 2026 Commerce Department letter ordered Anthropic to restrict two models, Mythos and Fable, for foreign nationals. Unable to verify citizenship per user, Anthropic disabled both for everyone; Fable stayed offline for 18 days and returned after the company agreed to report malicious activity, with the government retaining the right to reimpose restrictions.

The author's own experience: Writing as a heavy user, he describes building agent teams and roughly 1.5 million lines of AI-assisted code, running 171 automated jobs on a local Mac Studio with open models, and being refused by closed labs' tools for benign tasks such as collecting public drug package inserts — his argument for ownership over rental.

The surveillance argument: Quoting Anthropic's chief telling the Senate in 2023 that controlling a deployed model means being able to monitor its usage, the author pairs that statement with the government's switch-off power and reporting agreement to argue that closed models amount to a monitorable, revocable AI infrastructure.
report.impact: If the author's reading holds, the practical effect is a regulatory moat: compliance costs, mandatory disclosure of weights and training data, and per-day fines fall hardest on open releases and small labs, while closed providers with legal teams absorb them. That shifts competition from model quality toward distribution, licensing and government relationships. For developers, the lesson is portability — treat hosted APIs as revocable, keep an open-weight fallback, and avoid hard dependencies on a single provider's terms. For regular users, it means less choice, capability that can vanish by letter, and possible reporting arrangements behind the products they use. The counterargument deserves equal weight: officials frame these measures as national-security and safety controls, not market protection, and the article's causal chain rests heavily on the author's own inference.
report.tools: To follow the open-weight path the author advocates, look at Ollama and LM Studio for local model running, llama.cpp and vLLM for inference and serving, and Hugging Face for weights and licensing terms. Open model families to watch include Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek and Gemma. For agent work, examine Hermes Agent (cited in the piece), LangGraph and OpenHands. For policy tracking, follow Stanford HAI's AI Index, the EU AI Act implementation timetable, and Commerce Department BIS export-control notices.
